1.15.m: Bhīṣma said: / “What did Brahmā do, O brahmin, having sent [him] to the city of Vārāṇasī? / What deed was done by Janārdana and by Śaṅkara, O sage?
How was the sacrifice performed by him, and in which pilgrimage place? Tell me! / Who were the members of the assembly and the officiating priests? Tell me all of them!
Which gods were propitiated by him? This is a great wonder to me.” / Pulastya said: / “On the peak of Mount Meru is a city, a receptacle of splendour, adorned with jewels,
the abode of many wonders, crowded with numerous trees, / brilliant with varied minerals, pure as clear crystal,
rich in the beauty of canopies of creepers, resounding with the cries of peacocks, / filled with herds of elephants terrified by the roaring of lions,
cooled by showers of spray rising from cascading waterfalls, / variegated with serene pools beside groves of trees tossed by the wind,
with its entire forest perfumed by the fine fragrance of musk, / where traveling Vidyādharas, weary from amorous sport, slept in bower-dwellings,
resounding with the sweet melody of troops of singing Kinnaras; / therein, having all its grounds beautified with manifold arrangements,
was the dwelling named Vairāja, belonging to Brahmā Parameṣṭhin. / There, [the hall] resounded with the sweet song sung aloud by divine maidens,
garlanded with strings of flower-clusters born of the Pārijāta tree, / multicolored from clusters of rays arising from jewels,
having tens of millions of erected pillars adorned with spotless mirrors, / made radiant by the charming play of the dance movements of Apsarases,
resounding with the combined sound produced by many musical instruments, / beautified by numerous vocal and instrumental melodies accompanied by tempo and rhythm,
the assembly hall named Kāntimatī, bestowing happiness upon the gods, / attended by gatherings of ṛṣis, visited by multitudes of sages,
resounding with the sound of the Sāman chants of twice-born priests and giving joy. / Seated in it, the lord of gods, the Grandfather, intent upon the twilight worship,
meditated on the Supreme God by whom this universe was fashioned. / As he was meditating, the thought arose: ‘How shall I perform a sacrifice?
In what place should the sacrifice be performed by me? Where on the surface of the earth? / Kāśī, Prayāga, Tuṅgā, Naimiṣa, and Śṛṅkhala,
Kāñcī, Bhadrā, Devikā, Kurukṣetra, and Sarasvatī, / Prabhāsa, and other pilgrimage places here on the earth—
whatever sacred fields and holy pilgrimage places exist all around, / as well as the others made on earth by Rudra at my command—
just as I stand as the primordial god among all the gods, / even so I shall make one supreme, primordial pilgrimage place.
The lotus born from the navel of Viṣṇu where I arose / is proclaimed as the Puṣkara pilgrimage place by sages who recite the Vedas.’
While Brahmā Prajāpati was reflecting thus, / this thought occurred to him: ‘I will go to the surface of the earth.’
Reaching that ancient site, he entered that excellent forest, / crowded with various trees and creepers, adorned with diverse flowers,
filled with the calls of various birds, thronged with herds of various animals, / scenting gods and asuras with the fragrance of its heavy load of tree-blossoms,
its ground decorated with flowers that seemed deliberately placed, / with ripe and unripe fruits of diverse smells and tastes born in the six seasons,
fruits rich in golden form, charming to smell and sight. / Where the wind, as if out of kindness, throws out whatever
withered leaves, grass, dry wood, and fallen fruits are produced. / Gathering the perfume of clusters of diverse flowers,
the cool breeze blew, perfuming the sky, the earth, and the directions. / It was adorned with trees of numerous names, bearing crests,
green, glossy, free of holes, grand in a forest untouched by insects, / free of disease, handsome, well-rounded, and radiant—
resembling an assembly of brahmins with their officiating priests on every side. / Covered with sprouts resembling minerals, the trees shone
like men of noble lineage covered with their own flawless virtues. / With their tips shaken by the wind, they seemed to touch one another,
and, with their crest-garlands of flowering branches, they seemed to kiss one another. / In some places, nāgakeśara trees with their flowers, vanīra trees, and filaments
shone like eyes with moving black pupils. / In some places, karṇikāra trees with tops full of blossoms,
growing in pairs, two by two, shone just like husband and wife. / With the mass of their beautiful blossoms, rows of sinduvāra trees
shone like embodied forest deities being worshipped. / Here and there, kunda creepers, bright with their ornaments of flowers,
shone raised up on trees in all directions like crescent moons. / In some forest tracts, sarja and arjuna trees in bloom shone
like men clad in garments of washed silk. / Likewise, trees blossomed over with atimuktaka creepers
stood embraced like beloved men by their own women. / With their leaves intertwined with one another, sāla and aśoka trees
seemed like friends reunited after a long time touching hand to hand. / Bowed down by the weight of fruits and flowers, panasa, sarala, and arjuna trees
seemed to worship one another with flowers and fruits. / With the branches of the sāla trees joined by the force of the wind,
the trees seemed to rise up in greeting toward the people who had arrived near them. / Arranged for great beauty with an enclosure of flowers,
having reached the spring festival, they rivaled men; / with their crests bowed by the heavy beauty of blossoms and shaken by the wind,
they seemed like joyful men dancing, their heads adorned with garlands. / The trees, endowed with rows of flowers and tossed by the wind at the top of their crests,
danced with their creepers like men together with their beloveds. / The trees in some places, covered with creepers bowed by their own flowers,
shone like the autumn sky with variegated hosts of stars. / Or rather, flowering mālatī creepers on the tops of the trees
shone like crests fashioned with deliberate artistry. / The green trees, with golden sheen, were laden with fruit and flowers.
just like men showing friendliness upon meeting virtuous folk. / Bees, tawny from flower filaments, went in all directions,
as if proclaiming the triumph of the kadamba blossoms; / somewhere, drunk on floral nectar, they darted to and fro.
Flocks of male cuckoos stayed with their beloved mates in the thickets of trees; / somewhere parrots, resembling śirīṣa flowers, were seen in pairs,
uttering varied cries like honoured brāhmaṇas [reciting chants]. / Peacocks with variegated plumes, accompanied by their female companions,
danced in the outskirts of the forest, shining like skilled performers. / Flocks of birds chirping and calling out with diverse notes
made the charming forest all the more delightful. / It was teeming with various herds of deer, its birds ever rejoiced.
That forest, equal to the Nandana grove, gladdened both heart and sight. / And the lotus-born Lord, beholding that foremost forest of such beauty,
gazed upon it with a benevolent glance like a mirror, as if purifying it. / Then all those rows of trees, seeing the god arrived in that manner,
offered their abundant blossoms in devotion to Brahmā and shed them before him. / Accepting the flowers from the trees, the Grandfather
said to the trees: "Choose a boon! May good fortune attend you!" / Addressed thus by the Lord, the unrestrained trees,
all joined their hands in reverence, bowed to Viriñci, / and said: "If you grant a boon, O God affectionate toward those who seek refuge,
"then, O Lord, remain ever present in this very forest. / This is our highest wish, O Grandfather; homage to you!
"If you dwell in this forest, O Lord of gods, source of all creation, / then for us who have sought refuge with our whole being, desiring the supreme boon,
"away with ten million other boons—let [only this] boon be granted! / Through your presence, this [place] will become the greatest and foremost of all sacred fords."
Brahmā said: / "This sacred place shall become the most excellent and auspicious of all. / You will always be endowed with flowers and fruits, possessing perpetually stable youth.
"You will go where you wish, assume forms at will, and bestow fruits according to wish; / pleasing to the sight of men, shining through the ascetic accomplishments of human beings,
"and endowed with supreme splendour shall you become by my grace." / Having granted the boon in this way, Brahmā showed favour to the trees.
Remaining there for a thousand years, he cast a lotus (puṣkara) down upon the earth. / Struck by it, the earth fell down and the netherworld trembled.
Helpless, the oceans abandoned their shores, their waves agitated; / and thousands of mountain peaks, struck as if by Indra's thunderbolt,
crumbled away, though they were inhabited by tigers and serpents. / The aerial chariots of gods and siddhas and the cities of gandharvas
shook, wandered astray, fell down, and sank into the surface of the earth. / Pigeon-coloured clouds, appearing like masses of envelopes, dropped from the sky;
covering the celestial bodies, they became fiercely blazing. / By the mighty sound of that [impact], the entire three worlds,
with all that moves and is still, became bewildered, turned mute, blind, and deaf. / The bodies and minds of all the gods and asuras
sank in despair, and they could not fathom: 'What is this? What is this?' / Then, summoning their courage, all of them looked about for Brahmā,
yet they did not see him. 'Where indeed has Brahmā gone? / For what reason has the earth trembled, and why do these portents and omens appear?'
Just then, Viṣṇu went to the place where the gods were gathered. / Bowing down, the denizens of heaven addressed these words [to him]:
"What is this, O Lord? Tell us about the manifestation of these portents and omens! / By which the three worlds have been shaken, overtaken by the law of time,
"and the end of the kalpa has arrived, the oceans having breached their bounds! / What is this that the four elephants of the quarters and the immovable mountains have moved?
"Why has the earth suddenly been covered by the waters of the seven oceans? / O Lord, the occurrence of such a sound cannot be without a cause!
"Such a sound as has been remembered has never been, nor will ever be! / A terrible and fierce upheaval has thrown the three worlds into confusion!
"Is this sound auspicious or inauspicious for the three worlds and the denizens of heaven? / O Lord, if you know what this is, please tell us!"
Addressed thus, Viṣṇu, filled with supreme power, said: / "Do not fear, all you Maruts! Hear the cause of this:
"Having understood it with certainty, I shall tell it to you just as it happened. / Indeed, the Lord Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, holding a lotus in his hand,
"stood ready to perform a sacrifice upon a place on earth that is a heap of merit, / on the slope of the mountains, in a most beautiful forest.
"The lotus fell from his hand onto the surface of the earth; / this great sound is from that [impact], by which all of you have been shaken.
"There he was greeted by the cluster of trees with the fragrance of their blossoms; / and having bestowed his grace upon that forest, along with its deer and birds,
"the Lord chose to take up residence there for the welfare of the world. / That sacred ford is named Puṣkara, and it is indeed a supreme holy field.
"It was brought forth by the Lord who works the welfare of the worlds. / Having gone there indeed, satisfy Brahmā along with me.
"When propitiated, the Lord will grant excellent boons." / Having spoken thus, the Lord Viṣṇu, accompanied by those gods and dānavas,
went to that region of the forest where the lotus-born [Brahmā] was seated. / Joyful, satisfied in mind, accompanied by the songs of cuckoos,
they entered Brahmā's auspicious forest, bright with heaps of flowers. / That forest, reached by all the gods and resembling the Nandana grove,
rich in lotus pools, deer, and blossoms, shone exceedingly bright at that time. / Having entered the forest adorned with all kinds of flowers,
the gods wandered about, longing to see him, thinking: 'The god is here!' / Searching everywhere, all those gods along with Indra,
swift-moving though they were, could not find the end of that wondrous forest. / While searching for the god, the deities then saw Vāyu.
He said to them: "You will not see Brahmā without ascetic austerity." / Then, weary from searching repeatedly on that mountain ridge,
to the south, to the north, and in between, / taking Vāyu's word to heart, Vāyu spoke to them again:
"The means of seeing this Viriñci is always three-fold; / it is declared to be through faith, through knowledge, through ascetic austerity, and through yoga.
"Yogins perceive the god as both with form and formless: / ascetic practitioners see him with form, whereas those possessing knowledge see the supreme formless [aspect].
"Even when knowledge has arisen, one of feeble faith does not see him. / Yogins behold Brahmā quickly through supreme devotion.
"He, the changeless Lord of primal matter and spirit, is to be seen. / Ever joined in action, thought, and word toward the Grandfather,
"practise ascetic austerity—may good fortune attend you!—intent upon the propitiation of Brahmā. / For twice-born devotees who have undertaken the Brāhmī initiation,
"he always knows: 'I must grant my vision.'" / Having heard the words of Vāyu and realising this to be beneficial,
their minds possessed by the desire for Brahmā, they said to Bṛhaspati: / "O wise one among the gods, confer the Brāhmī initiation upon us!"
Desiring to initiate the immortals quickly with the Brahmā-initiation, / that preceptor initiated them according to the procedure declared in the Vedas.
Modest in attire and bowing low, they assumed the state of disciples; / having obtained Brahmā's grace, the knowledge related to Puṣkara was imparted to them.
Bṛhaspati, the best of the Adhvaryu priests, performed the sacrifice according to rule, / having fashioned a lotus endowed with stalks through the ritual application of the lotus initiation.
The sage, prompted by the will of the gods, showed grace to those gods; / being attentive to what is taught in the Veda, he gave to those discerning ones,
having abandoned amazement, the great-minded Bṛhaspati gave initiation; / and the noble-minded one, having consecrated a single fire for the dwellers of heaven,
being pleased, the son of Aṅgiras imparted the recitations prescribed in the Veda: / the Trisuparṇa, the Trimadhu, and the purifying Pāvamānī hymns.
Indeed, the generous-minded one instructed [them] in all the recitations and rites. / The bath [performed with the hymn] 'āpo hi ṣṭhā' is recited as the brāhma bath;
it destroys sin, calms the wicked, increases nourishment, prosperity, and strength, / bestows success and fame, and removes the impurities of the Kali [age].
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the brāhma bath. / Observing silence, self-controlled, initiated, with senses subdued,
all equipped with water-pots, their upper garments loose, wearing rosaries, / bearing staves, dressed in bark garments, and looking magnificent with matted locks,
intent upon bathing, right conduct, and seated posture, practicing meditation with effort, / fixing their minds upon the Brahman and desiring regulated food,
they remained devoid of seeing, conversation, company, or stray thoughts. / Thus observing vows, all bathing at the three periods of the day,
endowed with supreme devotion and supreme ritual order, / in time, through prolonged meditation, their minds attained knowledge of the god.
When their minds had become completely purified, consumed by the fire of meditating on Brahman, / the Lord appeared within the range of everyone's vision.
Overwhelmed by his splendour, their minds became bewildered. / Then courage was summoned, and according to rule, [before] the beloved god,
with glad hearts and intent upon him through the six-limbed Veda, / with folded hands placed upon their heads, and bowing their heads to the earth,
they praised the Creator, the Sustainer, the Supreme Lord. / The gods said: / 'To Brahmā, whose body is the Veda, who is friendly to brāhmaṇas, and who is unconquered,
well-restrained, we bow to the giver of sacrifices and the Veda; / homage indeed to the one compassionate to the worlds, whose form is the creation of the gods!
To the one exceedingly compassionate to devotees, praised with Vedic chants, / whose essential nature is manifold, who bears hundreds of forms;
homage to the lord of Sāvitrī, the divine lord of Gāyatrī! / Homage to you, who sit upon a lotus, who are the lotus, and whose face is like a lotus!
To the granter of boons, worthy of boons, to the tortoise, and to the deer, / to the one adorned with a diadem of matted hair, bearing the sruva and sruc ladles;
homage to you, whose mark is the hare, who possess the nature of a deer, the eye of dharma! / Homage, homage to the All-named, to the All, to the Lord of the All!
O eye of dharma, you ought to grant us protection greater than this; / with thought, word, and bodily posture, we have sought refuge in you, O Grandfather!'
Thus praised by the gods, Brahmā, the best of the knowers of Brahman, said: / 'Indeed, when remembered, I shall grant [it]; my vision to you is never unfruitful.
Speak what you desire, my sons; I shall grant excellent boons.' / Thus addressed by the Blessed Lord, the gods spoke these words:
'O Blessed Lord, this very thing today is an ample and great boon: / this great sound was produced for us when the lotus was cast by you.
For what reason was the earth shaken and the worlds agitated? / This is not without purpose, O Lord; let the cause here be told.'
Brahmā said: / 'This lotus was cast by me indeed for your benefit / and for the protection of the gods; hear the reason for this:
This demon Vajranābha, who steals away the lives of children, / having taken support of the nethermost subterranean world, was stationed there.
Knowing of your coming, that evil-doer wished to kill the gods together with Indra, / who were engaged in austerities and had laid down their weapons.
A blow was dealt to him by me with the dropping of the lotus; / he was arrogant because of royal power, and therefore he was slain by me.
In this world, at this time, may the devoted brāhmaṇas who have crossed to the other shore of the Veda / never go to an evil state; rather, let them attain an auspicious state.
Toward the gods, the Dānavas, humans, serpents, and rākṣasas, / toward the entire host of living beings, I am impartial, O dwellers of heaven.
For your benefit, that wicked one was slain by me with a sacred formula; / he has reached the worlds of the meritorious through the sight of this lotus.
Because the lotus was released by me, on earth this Puṣkara / shall become celebrated as a holy bath, purifying and bestowing great merit.
It is proclaimed to be the giver of merit to all living beings on earth. / Favor has indeed been granted to devotees who desire devotion, O gods.
By abiding constantly in this forest and being requested by the trees, / when I arrived, O sinless ones, Mahākāla did not depart from this forest.
And to you who are practicing austerities, great knowledge has been shown; / hold it in your hearts, O gods, both for your own sake and for the sake of others.
It should be seen by you on earth, assuming various forms. / A man who hates a wise brāhmaṇa is tormented by sin itself;
he will not be freed from sin even after hundreds of millions of births. / One should not kill or revile a brāhmaṇa who has crossed to the other shore of the Vedāṅgas;
for when one is slain, ten million are slain. / If one feeds a single brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedānta with faith,
ten million brāhmaṇas have been fed by him; of this there is no doubt. / Whoever offers alms that fill the bowl of ascetics
is freed from all sins and does not meet an evil fate. / Just as I am the eldest, the best, the Grandfather of all the gods,
so the man of wisdom, free from egoism and possessions, is always worthy of worship. / For the release of the bond of saṃsāra, this vow guarded by Brahman
was established by me for brāhmaṇas, causing the cessation of rebirth. / If one who has not conquered his senses undertakes the Agnihotra and then abandons it,
he goes swiftly to Raurava, led by the servants of Yama. / One who engages in wrangling over mundane life and performs base actions,
whose mind is attached to passion, who is amorous, fond of women and wealth, / who eats alone, enjoys delicious food, and engages in agriculture and trade,
who knows not the Veda, reviles the Veda, and consorts with another's wife— / from merely conversing with one defiled by such faults,
a man goes to hell; and also one who violates virtuous vows. / One who is discontented, fickle-minded, foolish, and performs sinful acts—
one should not touch him with bodily contact; if touched, one becomes pure through bathing.' / Having spoken thus, that Blessed Lord Brahmā, along with those immortals,
established the sacred precinct. I shall tell you in detail: / north of the Candrā river, as far east as the Sarasvatī,
and east of the Nandana, all the way to Kalpa, including Puṣkara. / This altar was indeed prepared at the sacrifice by Brahmā, the maker of the worlds.
The first is known as Jyeṣṭha, a holy bath that purifies the three worlds, / celebrated as having Brahmā for its deity; the middle one belongs to Viṣṇu,
and the lowest belongs to Rudra; Brahmā caused the first to be made. / This first, supreme sacred precinct is recited as a secret in the Vedas.
In the forest named Puṣkara, the Lord Brahmā is present. / Favor was indeed granted on this part of the earth by Brahmā himself,
for the sake of favoring all brāhmaṇas who walk upon the earth. / A raised platform bordered with gold and diamonds was fashioned from the earth,
built with diverse jeweled pavements, splendid in every way. / There sports the Blessed Lord Brahmā, the Grandfather of the world.
Likewise, the two gods Viṣṇu and Rudra, the Vasus, the two Aśvins, / and the Maruts along with Mahendra, as well as the gods of heaven, sport there.
This truth has been declared to you, the cause of favouring the worlds, / according to the sequence of the Saṃhitā, along with mantras according to the rules.
Those brahmins who recite the Vedas, devoted to serving their guru, / dwell in the proximity of Brahmā; they are all brought to majesty by him.
Bhīṣma said: / O lord, by what rule should men, residents of the sacred place, / who desire the world of Brahmā, reside in the forest of Puṣkara?
Should it be by men, or women, or those possessed of caste and stage of life? / What must be performed by those who dwell there? Tell me all of this.
Pulastya said: / It should be resided in by men and women living in the [proper] castes and stages of life, / devoted to the conduct of their own duties, free from hypocrisy and delusion,
devoted to Brahmā in action, mind, and speech, with senses subdued, / free from malice, not petty, and delighting in the welfare of all beings.
Bhīṣma said: / Performing what action is a man said here to be devoted to Brahmā? / And what are the devotees of Brahmā among men considered to be like? Tell me.
Pulastya said: / Devotion is declared to be of three kinds, arising from mind, speech, and body; / and it may be worldly, Vedic, and likewise spiritual.
That which, by the intellect characterized by meditation and retention, is the recollection of the meaning of the Vedas, / pleasing to Brahmā—this is called mental devotion.
Through mantras, Vedic recitations, prostrations, contemplation on the sacred fire, ancestral rites, and so on, / and through prayers and obligatory duties, it is recognized as verbal devotion.
Through observances and fasts with restrained minds and senses curbed, / through ornaments rich in gold and jewels, and likewise through Cāndrāyaṇa penances and the like,
through the Brahmakṛcchra penance, fasts, and likewise through other auspicious observances, / bodily devotion is described. For the twice-born it is threefold.
With cow's ghee, milk, and curd, with jewel-lamps and kuśa-water, / with various perfumes and garlands, and with offerings of minerals;
with incenses of ghee and bdellium, and with the fragrant scents of black aloe, / with ornaments rich in gold and jewels, and with variegated garlands;
with dance, instrumental music, and song, with offerings of all kinds of jewels, / and with foods to be chewed, eaten, and drunk—the worship that is performed by men
dedicated to the Grandfather, that is regarded as worldly devotion. / The devotion that is [performed] through Vedic mantras and sacrificial offerings is regarded as Vedic.
The agnihotra is to be performed on the new-moon day or the full-moon day; / praiseworthy is the giving of priestly fees, the sacrificial cake, and the preparation of the caru oblation;
the sacrifice, steady dedication, the drinking of Soma, every kind of sacrificial rite, / the prayers of the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, and the study of the Saṃhitā—
[when] these are performed according to the rule, that is called Vedic devotion. / Fire, earth, wind, space, water, the moon, and the sun—
whatever rite is performed dedicated to these, all that has Brahmā as its deity. / But spiritual devotion to Brahmā is situated as two kinds, O king:
one named after Sāṅkhya, and the other born of yoga. Hear from me that division. / Twenty-four are the principles in number, beginning with Pradhāna.
They are insentient, objects of experience; the Puruṣa is the twenty-fifth. / The Puruṣa is sentient, the experiencer, not the agent of that action.
The Self is eternal and imperishable, the presiding overseer and instigator. / The unmanifest Puruṣa is eternal, and the Grandfather is the cause.
The creation of principles, the creation of dispositions, and the creation of elements in their true nature: / enumerating these by counting, as well as the Pradhāna composed of the guṇas;
similarity of nature, measure, sovereignty, and the Pradhāna possessing different properties; / causality, the nature of Brahman, and desirability—this is spoken of.
The capacity to be directed belonging to Pradhāna—this is spoken of as diversity of property. / Brahman is the agent in all things, while the Puruṣa is non-active.
Consciousness in Pradhāna—this is spoken of as similarity of nature. / And the distinction of principles among the principles, and action and cause;
the purpose, and the sovereignty that is not to be directed according to the enumeration of principles— / 'There is an enumeration,' so it is stated by the wise who determine and ponder the reality.

Having thus heard in truth the collection of principles and the enumeration of principles,
and what is higher than the principle of Brahman, the wise know the reality.
This devotion practiced by Sāṅkhya followers has been made spiritual by the virtuous. / Hear also about the devotion born of yoga directed toward the Grandfather by devotees:
constantly intent on breath-control, possessed of meditation, with restrained senses, / eating food obtained by begging, observing vows, or with all senses withdrawn,
he should practice concentration in the heart, meditating upon the lord of creatures, / seated on the pericarp of the heart-lotus, with a red face and beautiful eyes,
with his face shining all around, wearing a sacred thread across his waist, / four-faced, four-armed, with hands granting boons and fearlessness.
The mental perfection born of yoga is remembered as the highest devotion to Brahmā. / One who possesses such devotion toward the god is called a devotee of Brahmā.
And hear, O king of kings, the livelihood that is traditional for residents of the sacred place, / which was spoken in detail of old in the presence of all by the god himself
for the brahmins at the assembly of Viṣṇu and the other [gods]: / devoid of mineness, devoid of egoism, free from attachment, free from possessions,
without affection toward the circle of kinsmen, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal, / constantly granting fearlessness to living beings through diverse rites,
constantly intent on breath-control, devoted to supreme meditation, / sacrificers, ever pure, devoted to the duty of ascetics,
knowing the rules of Sāṅkhya and Yoga, knowing dharma, with doubts severed— / those brahmins residing in the sacred place who sacrifice according to this rule
in the forest of Puṣkara, hear the good fruit for them when they die: / they go to imperishable union with Brahmā, which is very difficult to attain,
having reached which they do not obtain rebirth that brings death; / abandoning return [to saṃsāra], established in the knowledge of Brahman.
There is rebirth for others dwelling in the worldly stages of life. / One who, relying on the rule of the householder, is always devoted to the six duties,
sacrifices properly according to rule with mantras, invited to the sacrifice, / attains a superior fruit, free from all suffering;
and in all the worlds his movement is unhindered. / Endowed with divine sovereignty, mounted on his own vehicle, with his family,
in an aerial chariot possessing great splendor, shining like the newly risen sun, / surrounded by thousands of women, possessing an abode that moves at will,
he wanders unrestrained through all worlds as he pleases; / most coveted among men, best in all virtues, wealthy.
Fallen from heaven, he would be born in an illustrious family, handsome, / knowing dharma, devoted to dharma, and master of the meaning of all sciences.
Likewise, through the celibate student's life, and through serving the guru, / engaged in Vedic study, living on alms, with senses subdued,
always engaged in the vow of truth, diligent in his own duties, / [he is conveyed] by an aerial chariot abundant in all desires, sustaining all desires,
unhindered, like a second sun. / The troops named Brahmā, secret and highly esteemed,
of immeasurable strength and sovereignty, worshipped by gods and Dānavas— / he attains equality with them, endowed with equal sovereignty;
among gods, Dānavas, and mortals, his weapons become unresisted / for thousands of ten million years, and hundreds of ten million years.
Endowed with such sovereignty, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu. / Having dwelt [there] with such grandeur, when he falls again,
from the world of Viṣṇu he is born in the realms of heaven by his own action.
Reaching the forest of Puṣkara, established in the stage of studenthood, / by the study of the Vedas he dwells, or dies.
When dead, he departs in a celestial aerial chariot by his own splendor, / shining like the full moon, pleasing to behold like the moon.
Reaching the world of Rudra, he delights together with the Guhyakas; / he attains great sovereignty, lord of the whole universe.
Having enjoyed thousands of cosmic ages, he is glorified in the world of Rudra. / But falling again from that world of Rudra in due course,
ever rejoicing there, having enjoyed untainted pleasure, / he is born in the celestial house of twice-born men, in an exalted lineage.
Among men he becomes righteous, handsome, and an eloquent speaker, / possessing a body desired by women, a powerful lord of great enjoyment.
Observing the conduct of a forest hermit, avoiding cultivated produce, / his progress is unhindered throughout all the worlds.
Feeding on withered leaves and fruits, eating flowers, roots, and water, / [gathering grains] like a pigeon, pounding with a stone, or using his teeth as a mortar,
he should live by [such] means of livelihood, wearing garments of bark and rags, / with matted hair, bathing thrice daily, rid of faults, carrying a staff.
Or devoted to severe vows, even if a Śvapaca or another, / lying in water, practicing the five fires, exposed to clouds in the rains,
sleeping on the ground with insects, thorns, and stones, / devoted to standing postures and the hero-posture, sharing food, steadfast in vows,
eating wild forest plants, granting fearlessness to all beings, / ever devoted to acquiring dharma, having conquered anger and senses,
devoted to Brahmā, dwelling in the sacred site, the sage dwells in Puṣkara, / abandoning all attachment, delighting in himself, free from longing.
And he who dwells here, O Bhīṣma, hear what his destiny is: / with the brilliance of the morning sun, adorned with altars and pillars,
devoted to Brahmā, he travels in an aerial chariot that moves at will, / shining in the sky like a second moon.
Accompanied by troops of Gandharvas and Apsarases skilled in song, instruments, and dance, / united with Apsarases for hundreds of millions of years,
he goes unhindered to the world of whichever god he pleases; / by the grace of Brahmā alone, he shines in this place and that.
Falling from the world of Brahmā, he also goes to the world of Viṣṇu; / fallen from the world of Viṣṇu, he goes to the world of Rudra.
Falling even from that station, he is indeed born in the continents, / and likewise in other heavens, having enjoyed pleasures as desired.
Having enjoyed sovereignty among them, he is then born again among mortals: / he is born as a king or a prince, wealthy and happy,
handsome, fortunate, beloved, renowned, endowed with devotion— / whether Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras dwelling in the sacred site,
devoted to their own duties, O king, of good conduct, long-lived, / entirely devoted to Brahmā, conferring grace upon beings.
Those seekers of liberation who dwell in the great site of Puṣkara, / when dead, they go to the abode of Brahmā in magnificent aerial chariots,
resounding with flocks of Apsarases, moving at will, changing form at will. / Or if someone offers his own body into a blazing fire,
meditating on Brahmā, of great courage, he would go to the abode of Brahmā; / imperishable and eternal is the world of Brahmā for him, along with splendors.
Delightful, supreme above all worlds, it fulfills one's desired goals. / Those who give up their lives in the water at most holy Puṣkara,
for those great-souled ones too, O Bhīṣma, the world of Brahmā is imperishable; / they see directly the god who destroys all sorrow,
the god attended by all the immortals, accompanied by the hosts of Rudra and Viṣṇu. / Men—even Śūdras—who die through fasting in the forest at Puṣkara,
they depart from there in aerial chariots yoked with swans, brilliant as the sun, / rich in various gems and gold, sturdy, fragrant with perfumes,
with peerless qualities and others, echoing with the songs of Apsarases, / fitted with banners and flags, ringing with diverse bells,
endowed with many wonders, displaying sports and arts, / splendid, endowed with good qualities, drawn by excellent peacocks.
Wise men who have died through fasting delight in the world of Brahmā. / Having dwelt there for a long time, enjoying pleasures as desired,
having returned to the mortal realm, he is born rich in a Brāhmaṇa family, an enjoyer. / A person who performs self-immolation in dried cow dung in the forest at Puṣkara,
abandoning all worlds, he goes to the world of Brahmā; / he would dwell in the world of Brahmā as long as an eon's end should come.
He does not behold the mortal realm afflicted by its own actions; / his movement is unhindered across, upwards, and downwards.
Worthy of worship in all worlds, spreading renown, self-controlled, / knowledgeable in the rules of good conduct, charming to all the senses,
skilled in dance, instruments, and song, fortunate, pleasing to behold, / always with unfading flowers, adorned with celestial ornaments,
dark like the petal of a blue lotus, with blue curly hair— / flawless, slender-waisted women filled with all good fortune,
endowed with every sovereign quality, extremely proud of their youth, / women residing there attend to him and delight him in bed.
Awakened from sleep by the sounds of lutes and flutes, / he enjoys the pleasure of a great festival, difficult to obtain for the undisciplined,
by the grace of the god of gods, Brahmā, who brings about auspiciousness. / Bhīṣma said: / Conduct is the supreme virtue; those devoted to the virtues of the sacred site,
devoted to their own duties and proper conduct, having conquered anger and senses, / go to the world of Brahmā—this does not seem surprising to my mind.
And without doubt, twice-born men go to other worlds as well. / But without fasting at Puṣkara and without observance,
women, Mlecchas, Śūdras, birds, domestic animals, and wild beasts, / the dumb, dull, blind, and deaf, destitute of asceticism and observances—
tell their destiny, O Brāhmaṇa, who reside in Puṣkara. / Pulastya said: / Women, Mlecchas, Śūdras, domestic animals, birds, and wild beasts,
having died in Puṣkara, O Bhīṣma, they go to the world of Brahmā / with bodies of celestial form, in aerial chariots brilliant as the sun,
endowed with divine arrays, with excellent golden banners, / adorned with steps of gold and diamond and jeweled pillars,
filled with all enjoyable desires, moving at will, changing form at will; / thronged by thousands of women, they go to [a place] rich in various delights,
to the world of Brahmā, the great-souled ones, and to other worlds as desired. / And falling from the world of Brahmā, they go in due course to the continents;
in an exalted, expansive family, he becomes a wealthy twice-born man. / Those born in an animal womb—snakes, insects, and ants,
land-born, water-born, sweat-born, egg-born, plant-born, and womb-born— / whether dying with desire or without desire in the forest at Puṣkara,
mounted on aerial chariots brilliant as the sun, they go to the world of Brahmā. / In the terrible Kali age, creatures are impelled by sin;
by no other means in this [age] are dharma and heaven attained. / But those men who dwell in Puṣkara, devoted to worshiping Brahmā,
In the Kali age, they achieve their purpose; others suffer in vain. / The sin that a man commits at night with his five senses,
by action, mind, or speech, under the sway of desire and anger— / in the morning, having reached the water at Puṣkara,
and having approached the Grandfather, becoming pure, he is freed from that sin. / Beginning from the rising of the sun until its ascent is seen above,
meditating in what is called the mental [lake] by the yoga of Brahmā, he removes sin. / Having seen Viriñci at midday, a man is freed from sin.
Whatever sin he commits with his senses from midday until sunset, / he is released merely by the sight of the Grandfather at twilight.
Even if he enjoys all sense-objects like sound and the rest through desire, / one who dwells in Puṣkara devoted to Brahmā, established in austerity,
dwelling in the middle of the Puṣkara forest, eating the taste of sweet food, / even if eating three times a day, is considered equal to one who lives on air.
The men of virtuous deeds who dwell in Puṣkara / attain great enjoyments by the power of this sacred site.
Just as there is no other body of water equal to the great ocean, / so indeed there is no holy place equal to Puṣkara.
There is no holy place superior in virtues to the Puṣkara forest. / Now I will tell you of others who are stationed in this sacred site:
All the celestials headed by Indra, along with Viṣṇu, / the elephant-faced one, Kumāra, Revanta, and the Sun;
Śivadūtī, likewise the goddess Kanyā, and always Kṣemaṅkarī. / Enough with austerities and observances for those who perform auspicious rituals and worship!
Having performed vows and fasts, even great ones, elsewhere, / he who remains inactive in the superior Puṣkara forest,
attains the fulfillment of all desires—a twice-born who always stays right here / goes to the supreme, imperishable place equal to the Grandfather.
In the Kṛta age in twelve years, in the Tretā age in one year, / in the Dvāpara age in a month, O Bhīṣma, and in the Kali age in a day and a night,
that fruit is attained in the world by the dwellers in this holy place. / Thus it was spoken of old to me by the god of gods, Brahmā:
‘There is no sacred site on this earth superior to this; / therefore, with every effort, one should take refuge in this forest.’
A householder, a student, a forest dweller, or a mendicant: / all who act according to what has been taught go to the supreme state.
He who properly performs the duty belonging to a single stage of life, / free from desire and hatred, is honored in the next world.
For a fourfold ladder to Brahmā is established here; / having relied on this ladder, one is honored in the world of Brahmā.
For a fourth part of his lifespan, a student, free from malice / and skilled in dharma and purpose, should reside with his teacher or his teacher's son.
Surpassing the teacher's service in work, one who desires to become [learned] should study; / he should be a giver of fees, and when summoned, he should approach the teacher.
He should be the last to lie down and the first to rise in the teacher's house. / Whatever service and other tasks are to be done by a pupil,
having done all that saying ‘it is done’, he should stand by his side— / a servant who carries out everything and is skilled in all duties.
Pure, diligent, endowed with good qualities, he should speak an agreeable answer; / with steady gaze and controlled senses, he should look at the teacher.
He should not eat when [the teacher] has not eaten, nor drink when he has not drunk; / he should not sit while [the teacher] is standing, nor lie down before he has slept.
With open palms he should gently touch his two feet; / with the right [hand] he should press the right [foot], and with the left the left.
Greeting the teacher respectfully, he should speak, pronouncing his own name thus: / ‘I will do this, O venerable one, and this too has been done by me.’

Having made all this known and having offered the wealth to the guru,
he should perform it; and all that has been done should be reported again to the guru.
Whatever fragrances or tastes a student does not enjoy, / he may enjoy them after returning [home]: such is the determination in matters of dharma.
Whatever observances have been described at length for a student, / a devoted pupil of the teacher should embrace them all.
Having rendered satisfaction to the teacher according to his power, / the pupil should conduct himself by duty only in the non-vulgar stages of life.
The twice-born, eating begged food and sleeping on the ground, / having properly studied from the teacher's mouth one Veda, two Vedas, or the Vedas and their meanings,
having completed the observances for the Vedas diligently during the fourth part [of life], / having given the teacher his fee, should return home according to rule.
Joined with a wife endowed with righteousness, having invoked the fires, he should worship them; / a householder should pass the second part of his lifespan.
Four modes of livelihood for a householder were established of old by the sages: / the first possesses grain in granaries, the second possesses grain in jars,
the third is said to have nothing for tomorrow, and the fourth gleans like a pigeon. / Among these, each subsequent one is superior in righteousness and most victorious over the worlds.
One indeed subsists by six duties, another proceeds by three, / and a fourth twice-born by two: he is established in Brahman.
They do not declare any greater holy place than the observance of a householder: / he should not cook food for himself alone, nor slaughter an animal in vain.
Whether an animal or any living being, it is entitled to sacrifice through consecration; / he should never sleep by day, nor in the first and last parts of the night.
He should not eat between [the fixed] times, nor speak falsehood here; / and no twice-born should live in his house eating without being honored.
So also his guests are to be honored, who are remembered as bearing the oblations to gods and ancestors: / those bathed after vows of Vedic knowledge, learned in the Veda, masters of the Veda,
living by their own duties, self-restrained, performing rituals, ascetic; / for them, oblation to gods and oblation to ancestors are prescribed for worship.
For one who has departed with perishable things, who has strayed from his own duty, / who has abandoned the Agnihotra fire, or who acts falsely toward his teacher,
or who is intent on falsehood, there is no right to these two rites. / Sharing with all living beings is prescribed here;
likewise, [food] should be given by the householder to those who do not cook for themselves. / He should constantly be an eater of leftovers, and constantly eat nectar.
Nectar is the remainder of the sacrifice, a meal equal to the sacrificial offering; / he who eats what remains after everyone has eaten is called an eater of leftovers.

Devoted to his own wife, self-restrained, exceedingly diligent, with subdued senses, / he should not engage in dispute with the group of officiating priest, family priest, teacher, maternal uncle, and guests;
with the old, children, the sick, physicians, kinsmen, relatives by marriage, and relatives; / with mother, father, son-in-law, brother, son, wife,
daughter, and the servants. / Avoiding disputes with these, he is freed from all sins.
By overcoming these [contentions], he conquers all worlds, there is no doubt. / The teacher is master of the world of Brahmā; the father is lord of the world of Prajāpati;
the guest is lord of all worlds; the officiating priest is a lord based in the Vedas; / the son-in-law in the world of the Apsarases; kinsmen in the world of the Viśvedevas;
relatives by marriage and relations in the directions; mother and maternal uncle on the earth; / the aged, children, and the sick are powerful in the atmosphere;

the family priest is lord of the world of the ṛṣis; dependents are guardians of the world of the Sādhyas; / the physician is lord of the world of the Aśvins; the brother is protector of the world of the Vasus;
the wife is mistress of the world of the Moon; the daughter in the abode of the Apsarases; / the eldest brother is equal to the father; the wife and son are one's own body.
Servants, the class of slaves, and a daughter are supremely helpless; / therefore, reviled by these, one should always endure it without feverish anger.
The wise householder devoted to domestic duty, steadfast in righteousness, having overcome fatigue, / should not undertake many tasks; being righteous, he should undertake only a little.
Three are the modes of livelihood for a householder, and among them each is higher in beatitude; / and similarly they proclaim the system of the four stages of life mutually supported.
