1.15.m:
And whatever observances are prescribed for them, all should be performed by one desiring prosperity: / by those with grain stored in jars, by gleaners of grain-ears and scattered seeds, and by those resorting to the mode of pigeons.

And the kingdom in which these dwellers abide flourishes; / and he purifies ten ancestors going backward and ten going forward.

Even while following this householder's mode of life, one who practices without distress / would attain a destination equal to the realms of the Discus-Bearer [Viṣṇu].

Or rather, this destination is ordained for those with conquered senses: / heaven is the realm, the established foundation for self-restrained householders.

For this order was established by Brahmā; when one is freed from it, / having attained the second in due order, he is glorified in heaven.

I shall speak also of the third; listen to the forest-dweller's stage of life. / When a householder sees wrinkles and gray hair on himself,

and sees offspring born of his offspring, then he should take refuge in the forest alone. / For those exhausted by the vows of a householder and dwelling in the forest-dweller's stage,

let it be heard, O Bhīṣma—may good befall you—for those who are a refuge to all people, / who have turned away [from worldly pursuits] following their consecration and reside in sacred places,

for men endowed with the power of wisdom, possessing truth, purity, and forbearance: / spending the third portion of life dwelling in the forest-dweller's stage,
he should tend those very fires, sacrificing to the celestials, / self-controlled, of regulated diet, devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu.

Then, gathering only what is needed for the fire-offering and all the ancillary elements of sacrifice— / uncultivated rice and barley, wild grains, and remnant forest food—

he should offer sacrificial food in summer, even during the five cold periods. / Even in the forest-dweller's stage, these four modes of livelihood are remembered:
some eat immediately what is gathered; some store for a month; / some keep stores for a year, and some store for twelve years,
making provision for honoring guests and for the ritual system of sacrifice. / In the rains, they remain exposed to the clouds; in winter, they stay in water;
in summer, they perform the penance of the five fires; in autumn, they feed on nectar-food; / they roll on the ground, or they stand on the tips of their toes;
they spend their time standing and sitting, even when their garments are worn out. / Some use their teeth as a mortar; others pound [grain] with stones;
some drink boiled gruel only during the bright fortnight; / some drink it during the dark fortnight, eating in accordance with traditional precepts;
some live on roots, some on fruits, and some, firm in vows, on water; / those holding to the Vaikhānasa vow conduct themselves according to rule.
These and other diverse consecrations belong to those wise men. / And the fourth, based on the Upaniṣads, is regarded as common to all.
The forest-dweller and the householder continually proceed, one after the other; / in that very age, dear one, by the brāhmaṇas who perceived all truths—
Agastya and the Seven Sages, Madhucchandas, Gaveṣaṇa, / Sāṅkṛti, Sadiva, Bhāṇḍir, Yavaprotha, and Atharvaṇa,
Ahovīrya, and likewise Kāmya, Sthāṇu, Medhātithi, Budha, / Manovāka, Śinīvāka, Śūnyapāla, and Kṛtavraṇa—
these, skilled in sacrificial actions, attained heaven from there. / These possessed direct knowledge of dharma, as did the hosts of wandering ascetics.
Among the sages of fierce penance who perceived the subtleties of dharma, / having worshipped the Lord of the Gods, the brāhmaṇas resorted to the forest.
Having cast off fleeting illusion, the brāhmaṇas resorted to the forest; / indifferent to asterisms, unassailable, groups of departed [sages] are seen.
Worn down by old age and afflicted by disease, / they entered the fourth, the remaining stage, from the forest-dweller's stage.
Quickly performing the Sadyaskra rite and giving all his wealth as sacrificial fee, / sacrificing to the Self, gentle-minded, delighting in the Self, relying on the Self,
depositing the sacred fires within the Self and abandoning all possessions, / he should promptly perform sacrifices and the primary offering here at all times.
For those who sacrifice perpetually, the sacrifice proceeds within the Self; / he should properly abandon the three fires within the Self, by means of the Self, in an instant.
Whatever he may obtain and by whatever means, he should eat that without reviling it; / devoted to the forest-dweller's stage, he should cast off his hair, body hair, and nails.
Purified by his rites, he goes at once from stage to stage. / When a twice-born renounces after granting safety to all living beings,
his realms are luminous, and after death he attains infinity. / Possessing virtuous conduct, with impurities removed, he does not desire to wander either here or in the world beyond.

Free from anger and delusion, beyond peace and conflict, he remains indifferent, contemplating the Self; / untroubled even when others depart in the control of death, free from [attachment to] his own treatises, without mental confusion in his heart,

an unobstructed movement belongs to the self-sacrificer, free of doubt, devoted to dharma, and of conquered senses. / Listen now to the supreme fourth stage, superior to this, endowed with excellent qualities, which surpasses the three stages,
proclaimed as the ultimate refuge. / Having received the consecration from those two stages, listen with a focused mind to what is to be done after that,
for the sake of the Supreme Self, in truth: / having donned the ochre robe across the three ordered stages,
he who proceeds to the supreme state of unexcelled renunciation— / hear how he is to conduct himself, having renounced with that meditation.
He should practice dharma alone, without companions, for the sake of spiritual attainment. / He who wanders alone, seeing [truth], does not abandon [virtue] and is not diminished.
Without sacred fires, without a fixed abode, he should visit a village only for alms; / providing nothing for the morrow, the sage should be endowed with contemplative intent.
Eating lightly, of measured diet, he should partake of food only once; / an alms-bowl, the roots of trees, ragged garments, solitude,
and equanimity toward all living beings: this much is the mark of a mendicant. / In whom spoken words enter like dead bodies fallen into a well,
and do not return to the speaker, he may dwell in the stage of absolute isolation. / He should neither see nor hear what should never be spoken by anyone;
especially concerning brāhmaṇas, this should never occur in any way; / he should constantly speak only that which is favorable to a brāhmaṇa.
He should remain silent when censured, administering medicine to himself. / The one by whom space always seems full, though he is alone,
and by whom the empty seems crowded—him the gods know as a brāhmaṇa.
Clothed in anything whatever, fed on anything whatever, / and lying down anywhere whatever—him the gods know as a brāhmaṇa.
Afraid of people as of a serpent, of honors as of hell, / and of women as of a corpse—him the gods know as a brāhmaṇa.
He neither rejoices when honored nor grieves when dishonored; / bestowing freedom from fear upon all creatures—him the gods know as a brāhmaṇa.
He should not welcome death, nor should he welcome life; / he should merely await the appointed time, just as a hired laborer awaits his order.
His mind unassailed, self-subdued, his intellect unbroken, / a man freed from all sins would then go to heaven.
Granting safety to all beings, and having safety from all beings: / for him, released from the body, there is no fear from any quarter.

Just as all footprints of other foot-travelers
are subsumed into the elephant's footprint, so all cognitions are subsumed into the mind.

In this way, all dharma and purpose are elevated in non-violence;
he who resorts to violence is ever as good as dead.

Therefore, the non-violent man, rightly resolute, with senses restrained,
a refuge for all living beings, attains the supreme path.

Thus, for the wise man satisfied with knowledge, devoid of fear,
death has no greater hold, and he goes to immortality.

Freed from all attachments, standing like the sky, a sage
who acts pleasingly to Viṣṇu and is tranquil—the gods know him as a brāhmaṇa.

He whose life is for dharma, whose dharma is only for delight [in truth],
and whose days and nights are for merit—the gods know him as a brāhmaṇa.

Him who has abandoned undertakings, who neither offers nor seeks praise,
undecaying, his actions exhausted—the gods know him as a brāhmaṇa.

All beings delight in pleasure; all suffer manifold sorrows;
he who has become weary of their cycle of birth should perform rites with faith.

The gift of fearlessness given as a sacrificial fee to beings surmounts all gifts in this world;
he who first offers his keen body attains infinite fearlessness from all creatures.

With an open mouth he offers the oblation, and attains infinite stability all around;
from contact with his body, the All-consuming Fire went forth and pervaded all this.

Into the span of a hand, into the heart that has flowed inward, the sacrificer of the self offers with the breath;
what is offered in his Agnihotra, stationed in the Self, is offered in all worlds along with their deities.

Those who know the divine Creator, threefold and golden, as the supreme reality,
honored among all beings, capable gods, they go to immortality.

The Vedas, the object to be known, the entire ritual precept, the Nirukta, and the supreme reality—
all these he who knows in the Self of the body, all rites continually attend upon him.

He who knows that immeasurable, golden [sun] unattached to the earth and residing in heaven, at the end of its orb,
moving clockwise to the south in the atmosphere, its rays shining brightly, as located also in the Self—
He whose mouth protects this universe, that wheel of Time is placed in the secret cave [of the heart].

Because through its grace he attains the cosmic body and all worlds in this life,
by pleasing the gods in that [Self], he becomes truly liberated forever here.

Consisting of light, eternal, ancient, he lives in the world; approaching it with fear of worldly gain,
he from whom creatures feel no fear, and who never shrinks from creatures,

Blameless, reviling no others, that vipra alone sees the supreme in his own Self;
having removed delusion and cleansed impurities, he desires worldly gain neither here nor hereafter.

Free from wrath and delusion, looking equally upon a clod of earth and gold, with grief destroyed, transcending conflict and alliance,
free from censure and praise, indifferent to pleasant and unpleasant, wandering like a detached mendicant.

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, named “The Glorification of Residence in the Sacred Field,” in the first book, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.

1.16.m:
Bhīṣma said:
This supreme glorification of the pilgrimage site that has been told, O brāhmaṇa,
the pilgrimage site arose on the surface of the earth by the falling of the lotus.

Stationed there, by the Blessed Viṣṇu and by Śaṅkara,
whatever was done, O tiger among sages, declare all of that.

How was the sacrifice indeed performed there by the all-pervading god?
Who were the participants and priests, and which brāhmaṇas assembled?

What were the shares of that sacrifice? What was the offering material? What was the sacrificial fee?
What altar, and of what measure, was constructed there by Virañci?

He who is worthy of sacrifice for all the gods, who is everywhere recited by the Vedas—
meditating on what desire did the Creator perform the sacrifice?

For just as that lord of the gods is undecaying and immortal,
even so the heaven of that god is seen to be imperishable.

And heaven was granted to the other gods by that great-souled one;
the Vedas and medicinal plants were created for the purpose of the Agnihotra.

And whatever other beasts are on earth, all were created by this Blessed Lord
for the sake of the sacrifice—this is the Vedic revelation.

Therefore my curiosity is aroused having heard these words of yours;
taking which single desire as the aim, what fruit, and what conception,

was this sacrifice performed by him? You should explain everything.
And that woman named Śatarūpā is called Sāvitrī here.

She is proclaimed to be the wife of Brahmā, and the mother of the ṛṣis;
she gave birth to the seven sages beginning with Pulastya, and the lords of creatures beginning with Dakṣa,

and Sāvitrī gave birth to the Manus beginning with Svāyambhuva.
How did Brahmā, dear to the brāhmaṇa, having abandoned that lawful wife who bore sons,

chaste, highly fortunate, observing good vows, pleasantly smiling,
and faithful, obtain another wife?

What was her name? What was her conduct? Whose daughter was she, O lord?
Where was she seen by the god, and by whom was she shown to him?

What was her form, that goddess captivating the mind when seen,
beholding whom that lord of gods fell under the power of desire?

Surpassing even Sāvitrī in complexion and in beauty, O sage,
she who captivated the god, the all-pervading lord of all worlds.

How the god took that woman, the beauty of the world,
and how that sacrifice proceeded—tell all of that.

Seeing her at Brahmā's side, what did Sāvitrī do?
And what conduct did Brahmā then adopt toward Sāvitrī?

In their presence, what words were spoken to Brahmā by Sāvitrī
and what did she say again? You should tell all.

What was done there by all of you—anger or forgiveness?
Whatever was done there, whatever was seen, whatever has been asked by me here,

I desire to hear all the deeds of the Supreme Lord in detail and in full,
especially the supreme sacrificial ordinance of the Creator,

the order of rites, the beginning, and the hotṛ duties,
as well as the hotṛ's portion—to whom was the first portion granted?

And how did the Blessed Viṣṇu assist, by what means, and of what kind,
or what was done by the immortals? You ought to tell that, sir.

Having left the world of the gods, how did he arrive in the mortal world?
And how according to rule was the Gārhapatya, the Anvāhāryapacana on the south,

the Āhavanīya fire, the altar, and likewise the dipping ladle,
the sprinkling vessel, the offering ladle, and the concluding ablution bath arranged?

And how did he establish the three fires carrying sacrificial portions,
and make the gods eaters of oblations and the ancestors eaters of funeral cakes,

for the sake of their portions according to sacrificial ordinance, which sacrifices belong to the sacrificial rite,
the sacrificial posts, kindling wood, kuśa grass, soma, the strainer, and the enclosing sticks,

and sacrificial implements, as Brahmā made them?
He shone forth in ancient times through his actions as the Supreme Lord.

Moments, winks, kāṣṭhās, kalās, and the three divisions of time,
muhūrtas, lunar days, months, days, and years,

the seasons and the divisions of time, and the threefold measure of old,
lifespan, fields, decay, characteristic marks, and beauty of form;

the three social classes, the three worlds, the triple knowledge, the three fires,
the three divisions of time, the three rites, the three classes, the three qualities—
The higher worlds were created by the Creator, and whatever other [worlds are created] by one of small intelligence, / as well as the destination of the righteous and the destination of evil-doers;
the origin of the four castes, the protector of the four castes, / the knower of the four Vedas, the refuge of the four stages of life;
he who is heard of as the supreme light, who is heard of as supreme austerity, / who proclaimed the highest beyond the beyond, the supreme one who possesses the Supreme Self;
who is the dam among the dams of the worlds, the pure among pure actions, / the knowable among knowers of the Veda, the lord among masterly souls;
the breath of living beings, the fire of those endowed with the fire's splendor, / the mind of human beings, the ascetic heat of ascetics;
the modesty of those of prudent conduct, and the majesty of the majestic— / having thus created all this entirely, the grandfather of the worlds,
what goal did he seek from sacrifice? Why was his mind set upon sacrifice? / This is my doubt, O brāhmaṇa; this is my great doubt.
The supreme Brahmā is recited as wondrous by the gods and Daityas; / though wondrous by deed, he is truly declared right here.

Pulastya said:
This great burden of a question concerning Brahmā has been asked by you; / according to my capacity I shall speak—let that supreme glory be heard.
[He is] the one of a thousand faces, a thousand eyes, a thousand feet, / a thousand ears, and a thousand hands, imperishable;
possessing a thousand tongues, thousandfold, the supreme thousand-lord, / the giver of thousands, the first of thousands, thousand-armed, imperishable;
the offering, the pressing [of Soma], the oblation, and the hotṛ priest, / the vessels, the purificatory implements, the altar, the consecration, the caru, the sruva-spoon,
the sruc-spoon, the soma, the concluding bath, the sprinkling-water, the sacrificial fee; / the adhvaryu priest, the sāmaveda singer, the priest, the assembly members, the chamber, the assembly;
the sacrificial post, fuel, kuśa grass, the ladle, the cups, and the mortars, / the eastern hall, the sacrificial ground, the hotṛ, and whatever is bound,
short and exceeding measures, measures and immovable objects, / expiations, sacrificial portions, mounds, and kuśa grasses,
the mantra, the sacrifice, the oblation, the fire-portion, the origin, / eating first, eating the oblation, possessed of auspicious luster and raised weapons—
the brāhmaṇas who know the Veda declare him to be the eternal Lord, Sacrifice itself. / Concerning this sacred, divine story which you ask me, O great king,
as to why the blessed Brahmā performed a sacrifice upon the earth, / for the welfare of gods and mortals and for the origin of the worlds:
Brahmā, then Kapila, the supreme Lord, / the gods, the Seven Sages, and the far-famed Tryambaka;
and the exalted Sanatkumāra, Manu of great soul, the blessed Prajāpati; / then the ancient god, radiant like a blazing fire, initiated it.
Formerly, as he who was born from the lotus lay sleeping in its interior / at Puṣkara, where the gods and the hosts of sages arose,
this was the so-called manifestation at Puṣkara of that great-souled one, / where the Purāṇa well-combined with the Veda and Smṛti is related.
And the Boar, whose mouth was the Vedas, manifested from Brahmā; / for the sake of aiding [him], the best of gods assumed a boar's form.
Having made an extensive sacred ford at Puṣkara, Kokāmukha, beneficent, / having the Vedas as feet, the sacrificial post as tusks, the sacrifice as hands, the fire-altar as mouth,
having fire as his tongue, darbha grass as hair, the sacred formulation as head, performing great austerity, / having day and night as his divine eyes, the Vedāṅgas and Vedas as his ornaments,
having clarified butter as nose, the sruva-spoon as snout, the voice of the Sāman-chant as his loud roar, / full of truth and dharma, glorious, honored through ritual strides,

having expiation as claws, resolute, having sacrificial animals as knees, shaped like sacrifice, / with the udgātṛ priest as intestines, the homa as his phallus, having fruit, seeds, and great medicinal herbs,
having the wind as his inner self, mantras as bones, water as buttocks, soma as blood, / the Veda as shoulders, the oblation as fragrance, swift with offerings to gods and ancestors,
having the eastern hall as his body, radiant, worshipped by various consecrations, / with the sacrificial fee as heart, a yogin, composed of the great sacrificial session, magnificent,
delightful with the opening rite and iṣṭi offerings, adorned with the pravargya whirls, / accompanied by his shadow-wife, indeed lofty like a jeweled mountain peak,
he whose nature is the welfare of all worlds lifted up the earth with his tusk. / Then, having brought the earth to her own place, the bearer of the earth,
Hari, attained cessation from holding the earth. / Thus, held by the primeval Boar seeking the welfare of Brahmā,
the earth, which had fallen into the waters of the ocean, was lifted up of old at Puṣkara. / Accompanied by tranquil restraint and self-control, he who stood at the divine Kokāmukha,
together with the Ādityas, Vasus, Sādhyas, and Marut deities, / with the Rudras, with the All-gods, and with Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and Kinnaras,
with the cardinal and intermediate directions, the earth, the rivers, and the oceans, / the glorious Brahmā, teacher of the moving and unmoving, the foremost among knowers of Brahman,
spoke this word: 'O Lord, the sacred ford of Kokāmukha / must ever be guarded and protected by you; protection must be made here at the sacrifice.'
'I shall do so, O blessed one,' he then said to Brahmā. / Brahmā spoke once more to that god Viṣṇu standing before him:
'You alone are my supreme god, you alone are my supreme teacher, / you alone are my supreme abode, O best of gods among Indra and the rest!
O one with eyes like blossoming immaculate lotuses, bringer of destruction to the party of enemies! / In such a way that destruction of my sacrifice is not caused by the Dānavas,
and whatever Yātudhānas and Asuras are causers of obstacles at the end, / I will slay them all. Abide in peace, O Grandfather.'
Having spoken thus, he remained there, waiting for the moment to aid. / Auspicious winds blew, and the ten directions grew serene;
and the heavenly bodies shone brightly and circumambulated the moon; / the planets did not conflict, and the oceans became calm;

The earth became free of dust, and the waters granted all delight;
the rivers flowed on their own paths, and the oceans were not agitated.
the senses of men were auspicious in their inner self; / the great sages, free from sorrow, recited the Vedas aloud;
in that sacrifice, when the oblation cooked, the fires were auspicious; / their minds rejoiced, the people followed their rightful duties and good conduct.
Having heard the words of Viṣṇu of true promise concerning the destruction of foes, / then the gods arrived, along with Dānavas and Rākṣasas;
ghosts, departed spirits, and Piśācas—all came there in succession, / as well as Gandharvas, Apsarases, Nāgas, and the Vidyādhara hosts;
trees and medicinal herbs, whatever is here and whatever is not here, / were brought from all directions by the wind at Brahmā's command.
Having reached the sacrificial mountain around the southern direction, / all the gods stayed on the boundary mountain to the north.
Gandharvas and Apsarases, and sages who had mastered the Vedas, / occupied the western direction and remained there at that great sacrifice.
All the groups of gods, the Dānavas, and the hosts of Asuras, / setting aside their enmity, were exceedingly pleased with one another.
All attended upon the sages and served the brāhmaṇas; / sages, royal sages, twice-born, and celestial sages,
the most prominent royal sages, arrived from all sides, [wondering:] / 'Which god will be worshipped in this sacrifice?'
Beasts and birds went there eager to see, / and Brahmins desirous of eating, along with all castes in due order.
Varuṇa personally gave jewels, and Dakṣa personally gave food. / Having arrived from Varuṇa's world, cooked food spontaneously prepared itself.
The Wind cooked varieties of delicacies, and the Sun cooked savory juices; / the Moon made the cooking of rice, and Bṛhaspati bestowed intelligence.
The lord of wealth gave wealth and various garments; / the river goddess Sarasvatī was present, and goddess Gaṅgā along with the Narmadā,
and whatever other sacred rivers, wells, and bodies of water, / marshes, tanks, and various pools,
chief waterfalls, numerous trenches of the gods, / all reservoirs of water, and the seven oceans,
along with their waters of salt, sugarcane juice, liquor, clarified butter, curds, and milk; / the seven worlds with the netherworlds, the seven continents with their cities,
trees, creepers, grasses, vegetables, and fruits; / earth, wind, sky, water, and fire as the fifth,
the elements endowed with bodies, and whatever books of dharma, / commentaries on the Vedas, and sūtras, and whatever was fashioned by Brahmā,
the formless and the fully formed, all that is visible and embodied. / When that was thus arranged at that sacrifice of the Grandfather,
there in the presence of the gods and in the assembly with the sages, / on the right side of Brahmā stood eternal Viṣṇu.
On his left side stood Rudra, the wielder of the Pināka, the boongiver, the Lord. / And the choosing of the officiating priests was performed there by the great-souled one:
Bhṛgu was chosen there as the hotṛ priest, and Pulastya, the best of the adhvaryus; / Marīci was the udgātṛ priest there, and Nārada was appointed as the brahmā priest.
Those such as Sanatkumāra who were members of the sacrificial assembly were present there; / Dakṣa and the other lords of creatures, and the castes beginning with the Brahmins.
The appointment of the officiating priests was performed beside Brahmā. / They were endowed with garments and ornaments by Vaiśravaṇa.
Adorned with finger rings, bracelets, and diadems were the Brahmins— / the four, and the other twelve: the sixteen officiating priests.
They were all honored by Brahmā, preceded by prostration: / “I must be favored by all of you here in this sacrifice.
This Sāvitrī is my wife; O Brahmins, you are my refuge.” / Having summoned Viśvakarman, the shaving of Brahmā's head
was prescribed at that sacrifice, and caused to be done by the best of Brahmins; / garments of fine woven bark were likewise [brought] by the Brahmins for the couple.
With the chanting of the Veda, those Brahmins made heaven resound; / guarding this world, the kṣatriyas stood with weapons.
The vaiśyas prepared various kinds of edible delicacies there; / they prepared food to be chewed and food to be eaten, endowed with abundant flavors.
Having seen what had never before been heard or seen, the Lord of Creatures was pleased; / the all-pervading Creator gave the name “Prāgvāṭa” to those vaiśyas.
“Service to the feet of Brahmins is always to be performed here by the śūdras: / washing the feet, and cleaning up the remains of the meal.”
They too performed that there then. To them the Grandfather spoke further: / “For the sake of service, you have been placed by me in the fourth rank.
Service is to be performed by those such as you to the Brahmins, the kṣatriyas, and their kinsmen—to the three [higher castes].” / Having spoken thus, Brahmā did so.
Likewise, [he appointed] Śakra as superintendent of the door, Varuṇa as the giver of savory juices, / Vaiśravaṇa as the bestower of wealth, the Wind as the giver of perfumes,
the Sun as the provider of light; Mādhava stood in authority; / the Moon was their provider of Soma, taking his place along the left side.
And that well-honored wife, Sāvitrī, an excellent woman, / was called by the adhvaryu priest: “Come, O goddess, with haste!
All the fires have flared up, and the time for initiation has arrived.” / Distracted in performing her chores, by woman's nature she did not come:
“Indeed, nothing has been done by me here; no decoration at the doorway, / no multi-colored designs on the wall, nor any svastika in the courtyard.
The washing of the vessels has not been done at all here. / Moreover, Lakṣmī, the wife of Nārāyaṇa, has not arrived even today,
nor Svāhā, wife of Agni, nor Dhūmrorṇā, wife of Yama, / nor Vāruṇī, nor Gaurī, nor Suprabhā, the wife of Vāyu,
nor Ṛddhi, wife of Vaiśravaṇa, nor Gaurī, wife of Śambhu, beloved of the world, / nor Medhā, Śraddhā, Vibhūti, Anasūyā, Dhṛti, or Kṣamā,
nor Gaṅgā and Sarasvatī, nor have the young maidens arrived today: / Indrāṇī, the wife of the Moon, and Rohiṇī, beloved of the Moon,
Arundhatī, wife of Vasiṣṭha, and the wives of the seven sages, / Anasūyā, wife of Atri, and other ladies here,
daughters-in-law, daughters, female friends, and sisters— / none of them have arrived today, so I have waited a long while.
I will not go alone as long as those women do not come. / Go and tell Virañci: ‘Wait just a moment,
and accompanied by all of them, I will come in haste.’ / Surrounded by all, along with the gods, O wise one,
you will attain supreme splendor, and so will I, without a doubt.” / Leaving her as she spoke thus, the adhvaryu priest went to Brahmā:
“Sāvitrī is busy, O Lord, intent upon household tasks: / ‘As long as my female companions have not arrived, so long will I not come.’
Thus was I addressed, O god; and the proper time is passing away. / Whatever pleases you now, that do, O Grandfather.”
Addressed thus then, Brahmā, somewhat overcome with anger, [said]: / “Quickly bring another wife here for me, O Śakra,
so that the sacrifice proceeds and does not become deficient in its timing; / act swiftly in that way, and bring some woman!
Do not set your mind on her caste until my sacrifice is completed; / I will let her go again once the sacrifice here is finished.”
Addressed thus then, Śakra went through the whole surface of the earth; / and the women who were seen by him were all taken by others.
An Ābhīra maiden, rich in beauty, with a shapely nose and lovely eyes, / neither a goddess nor a Gandharva woman, neither an Asura maiden nor a Nāga maiden,
nor was there any maiden like that excellent woman— / he saw her of fair limbs, like another goddess Śrī,
diminishing the power of the mind's thoughts by the abundance of her beauty. / Whatever object of distinguished beauty may be found anywhere,
that choice quality was seen attached to the body of that slender-limbed girl. / Seeing her, he reflected: “If this girl should be [unmarried],
then no other god exists on earth who has acquired more merit than I! / This jewel of a woman is she; if the Grandfather is fortunate,
or if he should be passionate, then this effort of mine will be fruitful.” / He saw her possessing the luster of a dark cloud, gold, a lotus, and coral,
bearing brilliance with her limbs—hair, cheeks, eyes, and lower lip— / like a blossoming bud of the aśoka tree of the God of Love.
When the god of love was utterly burned by the mass of fiery flames from [Śiva's] eye, / how indeed was she created by the Creator who saw no match for her?
If she was conceived by his own intellect, it was the ultimate reach of his skill! / These two breasts with uplifted tips were fashioned such that joy arises in me as I look upon them;
in whose heart would wonder not arise? / Even though this lower lip has its body touched by passion, clearly...
Even so, it bestows liberation upon the one who serves it; / though bearing crookedness, pleasure is offered by her ringlets of hair.
Even a blemish shines like an excellence when it relies upon abundant beauty. / The two corners of her eyes, adorned, have extended to the vicinity of her ears.
Those who know the truth indeed proclaim that conscious presence arises from a cause: / the two eyes are the ear ornaments, and these two ears are [ornaments] of the eyes.
There is no room at all here for earrings and collyrium. / It is not proper that the side-glances should cause a split in the heart.
How can those related to you here share in sorrow? / Every change of form attains loveliness through natural qualities.
A boundless treasure has been seen by hundreds of matured gazes; / by the Creator, this frontier of skill in the production of beauty was clearly displayed.
With graceful sports, she endows the minds of men with affection." / As he was thus reflecting, his radiance captivated by her beauty,
his body became covered with horripilations that arose continuously. / Beholding her, radiant like fresh gold, with eyes long as lotus petals,
[he thought:] "Among the gods, yakṣas, gandharvas, serpents, or rākṣasas, / no woman possessing such wealth of beauty has ever been seen by me.
Gathering whatever foremost thing exists within the three worlds, / the Creator formed the composition of her beauty."
Indra said: / "Who are you, whose [daughter] are you, and whence have you come, fair-browed one? Tell me. / And why do you stand alone in the midst of the streets?
These ornaments placed upon your limbs which you wear— / they are not for your ornamentation, for you are indeed the ornament to them!
No goddess, no gandharva woman, no asura woman, no serpent maiden, / nor any kinnara woman has been seen before like you, fair-eyed one!
Though spoken to repeatedly by me, why do you give no answer?" / Filled with shame, that maiden, trembling, said to Śakra:
"I am a cowherd maiden, O hero; I sell cow's produce here. / Here is pure fresh butter, and here is curd free from watery scum.
With curd, and with buttermilk, and with essence, O tormentor of foes, / state whatever you desire; take as much as you wish!"
Being spoken to thus, Śakra then grasped her firmly by the hand, / and brought that large-eyed maiden to where Brahmā was present.
Being led away by him, however, she cried out to her father and mother: / "Ah, father! Mother! Ah, brother! This man is carrying me away by force!
If you have any need of me, ask my father; / he will certainly give me to you; the truth is being spoken to you.
What maiden would not desire a husband devoted to loving care? / Yet nothing is to be given to you without my father, O lover of dharma!
Propitiate him with bowed head; he, being pleased, will give me. / If I give myself to you without knowing my father’s mind,
great dharma would surely be destroyed; therefore I do not consent to you. / I will come under your control if my father will give me."
Being addressed in this manner, Śakra, however, led her away, / and placing her before Brahmā, said: "For his sake, O girl,
you have been brought, large-eyed one; do not grieve, fair-complexioned lady!" / Seeing that cowherd maiden of fair complexion and great splendor,
he regarded her as Kamalā herself, with eyes resembling white lotuses, / possessing full breasts resembling an excellent wall of molten gold,
with thighs round like the trunk of an elephant in rut, with the radiance of reddish, prominent nails. / Seeing him, she too thought of herself as walking in the wake of Kama.
Her mind seemed gone with the thought of the means to attain him; / the cowherd girl too deemed herself to have sovereignty in giving herself:
"If he, on account of my beauty, eagerly desires to take me, / there is no woman on earth more fortunate than I.
I was brought by this one and have come within range of his sight; / in being abandoned by him there would be death, in not being abandoned, a happy life.
And from disrespect I would become one whose beauty is ruined, a bringer of sorrow; / but even that woman who is seen by this eye through his favor,
she too is fortunate, without doubt; how much more so the one whom he would embrace! / All the beauty of the world indeed followed separate paths;
that charm has been displayed here assembled in one place by the source of the universe. / Kama is the fitting comparison for him, and the comparison for Kama's splendor is [his] splendor.
This grief is cast aside; father and mother are no consideration. / If he does not accept me, or speaks very little to me,
from remembering him, death born of sorrow will come to pass. / But when an innocent wife has departed quickly, such a one,
with a radiance equal to a pure lotus, for the adornment of a jewel upon her breasts— / as I behold his face, my mind has entered into meditation.
If you do not think highly of the contact of touching his limb, / then wandering about touching [others], you have an utterly useless body.
Or rather, he is not at fault, for you wander about at will. / You have certainly been robbed, O Kama! Protect your own beloved Rati!
For by his beauty he is seen to surpass Kama, even compared to you. / By him, the jewel of my mind, all that is mine, has been firmly stolen.
Whence could that splendor seen in his face exist in the moon, the hare-marked one? / No comparison is praised of that which has a blemish with that which is spotless.
A lotus does not attain equality with his two eyes; / what comparison could be attained by a water conch with the conches of his ears?
Even coral certainly does not find a comparison to his lower lip; / for he, dripping with the nectar abiding within himself, surely stirs.
If any auspicious deed has been performed by me across hundreds of other births, / by its favor, may he become my desired husband!"
While that cowherd maiden was thus consumed with thoughts, / Brahmā then spoke words quickly to Hari for the sake of the sacrifice:
"And this illustrious goddess is Gāyatrī by name, O Lord." / When this was spoken, Viṣṇu then said this to Brahmā:
"Therefore, marry her today, given by me, O Lord of the universe, / by the Gāndharva marriage rite; do not hesitate for long!
Take this hand of hers today, O God, without agitation!" / The Grandsire married her by the Gāndharva marriage rite.
Having obtained her then, Brahmā spoke to the best of adhvaryu priests: / "She has indeed been made my wife by me; usher her into my abode."
Holding a deer horn, veiled in silken cloth, the maiden / was then led to the patnīśālā by the officiating priests who had mastered the Vedas.
With a staff of audumbara wood, wrapped in a deerskin, / Brahmā then shone by his own splendor at the great sacrifice.

And then the hotṛ rites were begun by the brāhmaṇas who had mastered the Vedas; / together with Bhṛgu, the ritual prescribed in the Vedas was performed by them then. / And that sacrifice at Puṣkara continued for a thousand yugas.

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, named 'The Acceptance of Gāyatrī', in the first book, the Sṛṣṭikhaṇḍa, of the glorious Padma Purāṇa.
